title: Object-Oriented Programming as a Paradigm
summary: OOP as a paradigm-level mental model — objects bundling state and behavior, messages instead of calls, dynamic dispatch — separate from SOLID, patterns, and design, which live elsewhere.

slides.markdown:
Object-oriented programming is often taught as a bag of rules — classes, inheritance, `private` keywords — before anyone explains the actual idea underneath. The idea is simple: instead of separate data and the functions that operate on it, **bundle state and behavior together into one unit, and compute by having units send each other messages.**

Everything else — encapsulation, dynamic dispatch, class hierarchies — is machinery built to make that one idea work at scale. This Topic covers OOP as a *paradigm*: how it structures computation differently from imperative or functional code. The deep design discipline that comes with it — SOLID, design patterns, UML — is a separate skill covered elsewhere; here you're learning the mental model, not the rulebook.

slides.subTitle: Objects sending messages
slides.markdown:
In procedural code, data is passive: a `struct` sits there while free-floating functions like `calculateArea(shape)` operate on it. OOP inverts this — the `shape` **is** an object that knows how to compute its own area, and you ask it to: `shape.area()`.

Alan Kay, who coined the term, described the essence of OOP not as classes or inheritance but as **objects communicating by sending each other messages**, each object deciding for itself how to respond. `shape.area()` isn't "call the `area` function and pass `shape` as an argument" — conceptually it's "send the message `area` to `shape` and let `shape` decide what that means."

That distinction — data deciding how to respond to a request, rather than a function deciding what to do with data — is the actual paradigm shift. Classes, inheritance, and access modifiers are just one popular implementation of it (Smalltalk's, inherited by Java and C++); they are not the idea itself.

slides.subTitle: Not just "private fields"
slides.markdown:
Encapsulation is usually taught as "mark your fields `private`." That's the mechanism, not the point. The point is an **information-hiding contract**: an object exposes a set of operations (its public interface) and hides everything about *how* those operations are implemented, so callers depend only on the contract and never on the internal representation.

This matters because it lets the implementation change without breaking callers. A `Stack` can switch its internal storage from an array to a linked list; if every caller only ever used `push`/`pop`/`peek`, nothing outside the class needs to change. If callers had reached into a public field to manipulate the array directly, the swap breaks every one of them.

So the real test of encapsulation isn't "are the fields private" — a class with private fields but public getters and setters for every one of them has technically hidden nothing; callers can still read and write the exact internal state, just through an extra layer of indirection. The test is: **can the internal representation change without any caller's code changing?**

slides.sectionTitle: Message passing vs a function call
slides.markdown:
Side by side, the two models look almost identical in syntax but differ in who decides what happens.

In imperative code, `calculateArea(shape)` is a single, statically known function — the call site and the code that runs are the same piece of code, fixed at compile time. In OOP, `shape.area()` is a message sent to `shape`; *which* code runs depends on `shape`'s runtime type, not on the call site. A `Circle` and a `Rectangle` both receiving the message `area()` each run their own code — the caller never has to know which.

That indirection — same message, different code depending on the receiver — is what the next Subtopic calls dynamic dispatch, and it's the mechanical difference that message-passing buys you over a plain function call.

slides.subTitle: The same call resolving to different code
slides.markdown:
Dynamic dispatch is the mechanism that makes `shape.area()` route to the right implementation without an `if`/`else` chain checking `shape`'s type. Each object carries (directly, or via its class) a reference to a **dispatch table** — a lookup from method name to the actual code that implements it for that object's specific type.

When you call `shape.area()`, the runtime looks up `area` in `shape`'s dispatch table and jumps to whatever is there — `Circle`'s implementation if `shape` is a `Circle`, `Rectangle`'s if it's a `Rectangle`. The calling code never branches on type; the *object* supplies the branch, implicitly, through which table it points to.

This is what lets you add a new `Triangle` class later without touching any code that calls `.area()` — the new class supplies its own table entry, and every existing call site picks it up automatically the first time a `Triangle` flows through it. That property — extend behavior by adding a new type, not by editing existing code — is the paradigm's central promise, and it's the mechanism behind polymorphism.

slides.subTitle: Two different object models
slides.markdown:
"Object-oriented" doesn't imply classes — it implies objects sending messages, and there are two mainstream ways to get objects.

| | Class-based (Java, C++) | Prototype-based (JavaScript) |
|---|---|---|
| **Where behavior lives** | A class, defined separately from instances | Another object, called the prototype |
| **How a new object gets methods** | Instantiate a class | Link to (inherit from) a prototype object |
| **Can you change one object's shape alone?** | No — all instances share the class definition | Yes — you can add a method to a single object |
| **Relationship model** | "is-a" via class hierarchy | "delegates-to" via the prototype chain |

JavaScript objects don't have classes underneath in the classical sense — `class` syntax in modern JS is sugar over prototype linking. When `obj.method()` doesn't find `method` on `obj` directly, the runtime walks up `obj`'s prototype chain until it finds one (or fails). Both models deliver dynamic dispatch and encapsulation; they differ in where the shared behavior is defined and how flexible individual objects can be.

It's worth being explicit about what this Topic does and doesn't cover, because "OOP" gets used to mean several different things in interviews.

Here, OOP is a **paradigm-level mental model**: bundling state and behavior, encapsulation as a contract, dynamic dispatch, and the class/prototype distinction. What it does *not* cover: the SOLID principles, the Gang-of-Four design patterns, UML notation, or deep composition-vs-inheritance architecture guidance — that is application-design discipline built *on top of* OOP, not the paradigm itself, and it lives as its own dedicated material.

Why the split matters practically: you can understand every idea in this Topic and still write badly-designed OOP code, the same way knowing imperative programming's rules doesn't make your control flow well-structured. The paradigm gives you the primitives (objects, messages, dispatch); good design is a separate, learnable skill about how to arrange those primitives well.

Inheritance looks like free code reuse: `Duck extends Bird extends Animal`, and `Duck` gets `fly()` and `eat()` for free. The trap appears when a later requirement doesn't fit the hierarchy — say `RubberDuck extends Duck`, which shouldn't `fly()`, or `Penguin extends Bird`, which also shouldn't. You either override `fly()` to throw, or restructure the whole tree, and every level of a deep hierarchy makes both options worse.

The deeper problem: inheritance couples a subclass to its entire ancestor chain's implementation, not just its interface. Change how `Bird` stores its weight field, and every subclass three levels down may silently break, because they were relying on inherited implementation details, not a contract.

"Favor composition over inheritance" became conventional wisdom because composition — a `Duck` *has a* `FlightBehavior` object it delegates to — lets you swap behavior per instance (a `RubberDuck` gets a `NoFlight` behavior) without touching the class hierarchy at all, and without any implementation coupling beyond the one delegated interface.

Take "compute the area of a shape" — the running example from earlier — and see how the decomposition differs by paradigm, not just the syntax:

- **Procedural:** one function, `calculateArea(shape)`, containing an `if shape.type == "circle": ... elif shape.type == "rectangle": ...` branch. Adding a new shape means editing this function to add another branch.
- **OOP:** each shape class owns its own `area()` method; `calculateArea` doesn't exist as a separate function at all. Adding a new shape means adding a new class; no existing code changes.

The procedural version centralizes all shape-area logic in one place — easy to see everything at once, but every new case means editing shared code (a merge-conflict magnet on a team). The OOP version spreads the logic across classes — harder to see everything at once, but each addition is isolated. Neither is universally "better": procedural centralization suits code that rarely gains new cases; OOP's open-for-extension shape suits code where new cases arrive constantly and independently.

This question shows up often enough to prepare for directly. The honest answer is "multi-paradigm, with real OOP support" — not a yes/no.

Python has classes, inheritance, dynamic dispatch, and encapsulation-by-convention (a leading underscore signals "private," but nothing enforces it) — every object-model feature is present, just with weaker access control than Java. JavaScript has objects and dynamic dispatch via the prototype chain even without a single `class` keyword being used, which is why it was "object-oriented" for over a decade before ES6 added `class` syntax at all.

What neither language forces is that *everything* be an object — both support free functions and primitive values outside any class, which Java (mostly) and Smalltalk (strictly) don't. So the accurate framing: OOP is a paradigm a language can *support*, to different degrees of strictness, alongside other paradigms in the same codebase — not a binary property a language either has or lacks.
